title: Barriers to Counterfactual Credit Attribution for Autoregressive Models
one_liner: Autoregressive models that need to give credit to training data face two fundamental barriers that make credit attribution hard in ways that differ from privacy protection.
lead: When a generative model outputs text, it should credit the works it learned from. Counterfactual credit attribution formalizes this idea: given a model's output, could you pinpoint exactly which training examples were essential to produce it? This paper shows that for autoregressive models—the kind that generate text one word at a time—two natural approaches to this problem hit fundamental walls.

problem.h2: Why autoregressive models need to say thank you
paras: A generative model—say, a system that writes essays—learns from millions of training examples. When it produces an output, some of those examples were essential, others irrelevant. The question: can we formally say which ones? This is called credit attribution: if the model's output depends on a specific training example, the example deserves credit.

A naive approach: just take the finished model and ask it to mark which examples it used. But the model was never designed to track this, and forcing it to report honestly is hard—the model might lie to cover its tracks.

Another naive approach: rebuild the model without a suspect training example and see if the output changes. But this is expensive: for a long output (100 words), you might need to retrain the model 100 times, once without each word.

callout.b: The paper's move in one sentence.
callout.html: The paper proves these two ideas hit mathematical walls: word-by-word credit attribution cannot simply be built by making each individual word-prediction step credit its inputs, and retrofitting credit onto a finished model requires exponentially many queries.

steps.text: A model deserves credit only for examples it genuinely relied on to produce its output
If each word-prediction step is individually credit-aware, does combining them yield credit-aware full text? No.
Credit assigned at one word-prediction step can contradict credit at another, making the full output incoherent
Take a pre-built model, add credit-tracking to it by querying the original model without certain examples
To isolate which examples mattered for a 100-word text, checking all subsets of examples needs exponentially many model runs

paras: The paper does not propose a new model or method. Instead, it proves that two direct approaches to the problem—plugging in credit rules at each step, and bolting credit onto a finished model—hit fundamental barriers that no clever engineering can circumvent.

hidden.name: whether credit rules combine recursively
paras: When the model predicts word 2, it depends on word 1's output and the original data. Does word 2's credit for its sources plus word 1's credit for its sources give a coherent credit assignment for the full two-word text? In privacy protection, the answer is yes—privacy bounds compose cleanly. In credit attribution, the paper shows the answer is no.

The paper measures this by tracking which training examples are reported as sources at each step and checking whether a single training example can be credited at step 1 but discharged at step 2, creating a logical contradiction.

heat.caption: Darker means more tension; checked items show contradictions; credit at one step contradicts the next

reads.html: Imagine a student answers question 1, then uses that answer to solve question 2. If question 1 depends on textbook page 5, does question 2 also owe credit to page 5? In autoregressive models, the answer flips between yes and no at different steps, making the full credit assignment incoherent.
CCA does not compose autoregressively: given a model that generates autoregressive sequences, imposing CCA on each one-step predictor does not guarantee the full sequence satisfies CCA.

paras: An autoregressive model is a chain: data flows to word 1, then to word 2, then to word 3. Each step takes the previous words as input. If you want the full chain to give correct credit, you might think: make each step give correct credit to its own inputs, and let credit propagate. But that fails because of a conflict. Training example X might be essential for word 1's prediction, making word 1 credit X. But word 2's prediction might depend on word 1 itself, not directly on X. So word 2 might credit word 1 but not X. Now the final text credits word 1 but not X, yet word 1 credits X. This creates a phantom: X's influence is hidden inside word 1. The paper shows this contradiction is unavoidable—credit rules cannot compose step-by-step in autoregressive models the way they do in privacy.

The retrofitting barrier is different. Suppose you have a finished model that gives no credit at all. You want to add credit-tracking to it without retraining. One way: ask the model what happens if you remove training example X. Does the output change? If yes, X matters. But checking all possible subsets of examples—which ones individually or together matter—requires checking up to 2 to the N possible subsets, where N is the number of words the model generates. For a 100-word text, that is 2 to the 100, an astronomical number. No shortcuts exist.

stages.s: predict word 1: attributes credit to example X
predict word 2: uses word 1 as input; ignores X directly
words 1 and 2 combined: X credited at step 1, ignored at step 2
final text with contradictory credit assignments

math.words: To verify that training example X is essential for the full output, check if the output changes when X is removed. To identify ALL essential examples, check all 2 to the N possible subsets of N examples.
math.equation: queries_needed = 2^N, where N is the number of training examples to audit
symbols: number of training examples under consideration
exponential growth: doubling N quadruples the cost

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: If you have 10 examples to audit: 2^10 = 1,024 queries needed.
If you have 20 examples: 2^20 = 1,048,576 queries needed.
If you have 100 examples (a short text): 2^100 ≈ 10^30 queries needed—more than atoms in the universe.
No algorithm can avoid this cost; it is a fundamental barrier.

math.note: The exponential cost shows that retrofitting credit onto a finished model is impractical for any realistic text length.

charts.title: Composition attempt
charts.note: Credit rules assigned at each word-step contradict each other in the full sequence; no way to reconcile them.

charts.title: Retrofitting attempt
charts.note: Identifying which examples matter requires querying all possible combinations; cost explodes exponentially.

items.html: If you make each word-prediction step credit its inputs honestly, the credit assignments at different steps will contradict each other. An example marked essential at word 1 might be marked irrelevant at word 2.
Adding credit-tracking to a finished model by querying it without suspect examples requires exponentially many queries. For a 100-word text, this is computationally impossible.

These are not engineering problems that better algorithms can solve, because the composition failure stems from the logical structure of autoregressive prediction itself—each step depends on all earlier steps, creating unavoidable contradictions when credit rules try to flow backwards. Similarly, retrofitting's cost is unavoidable because the exponential number of subsets is inherent to identifying which elements in a set matter.

items.b: Radically different designs might escape both barriers.
items.html: The paper does not rule out entirely different model architectures—only direct adaptations of existing techniques.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a tiny autoregressive model on a small dataset (e.g., predicting 3-word sequences from a set of 10 training examples). Implement both approaches: (1) assign credit at each word-prediction step and try to combine them; (2) retrofit credit by querying the model. Show that approach 1 produces contradictions (an example marked essential at step 1 but irrelevant at step 2) and approach 2 requires checking exponentially many subsets of training examples.
demo.metric_eq: composition_failure = count of contradictions where example X credited at step i but discharged at step j; retrofitting_cost = number of model queries needed to identify all essential examples grows exponentially with text length
demo.closing: The demo must make it impossible to ignore: you cannot fix these barriers by tweaking hyperparameters or engineering tricks. They are baked into how autoregressive models work.
